metadata.name: airef-site-registry
metadata.build_method: Curated from accessible AIRef pages and search-visible summaries. Dynamic tables on AIRef are JS-driven, so this registry captures the stable page structure, definitions, and lookup routes first.
coverage_notes: This is not a full export of every AIRef command, parameter, or strategic number row.
Use this registry as startup context and navigation metadata, then drill into the cited AIRef pages for details.
Promote an entry from 'documented' to stronger local guidance only after it is validated by the linter and an isolated in-game probe.

commands.definition: Executable AI scripting primitives. Most day-to-day .per work is selecting, composing, and sequencing commands.

parameters.definition: Typed inputs and outputs attached to commands. Understanding parameter direction and type is mandatory for reading syntax correctly.

strategic_numbers.definition: Built-in mutable settings that steer AI engine behavior. Some are active behavior switches, some are effectively free storage.

duc.definition: Direct Unit Control. UserPatch-origin unit selection, filtering, point targeting, object targeting, and search-list manipulation.

tables.definition: Reference tables for object IDs, technology IDs, lines, sets, classes, and version-specific variants.

guides.definition: Narrative AIRef articles that explain semantics, pitfalls, and performance tradeoffs around the raw reference entries.

concepts.name: Commands
concepts.definition: Commands are the core units of AoE2 AI scripting. They make up most .per logic and are always written inside rules.
details: AIRef classifies commands by category, complexity, type, and version.
There are facts, actions, and a smaller set of commands that can behave as either fact or action.

concepts.name: Facts
concepts.definition: Facts are rule conditions. They must evaluate true before the actions section runs.
details: Facts appear before the => separator.
Example from AIRef: can-afford-building is a fact.

concepts.name: Actions
concepts.definition: Actions are rule effects. They execute only after all facts in the rule are true.
details: Actions appear after the => separator.
Example from AIRef: buy-commodity is an action.

concepts.name: UserPatch Facts/Actions
concepts.definition: UserPatch-origin commands, typically prefixed with up-, extend base AI scripting with DUC, advanced queries, and extra control surfaces.
details: AIRef notes that some UserPatch commands can be used as either a fact or an action.
If placed in the facts section, some of these commands can both validate and execute.

concepts.name: Parameters
concepts.definition: Parameters customize command behavior. A command can have zero to four parameters, and every populated parameter must use a valid value for its type.
details: AIRef's command syntax shows both direction and type prefixes per parameter.
Examples include player selectors, object IDs, goals, strategic numbers, and operators.

concepts.name: Parameter Directions
concepts.definition: Direction prefixes describe whether a parameter is used as input, output, or both.
details: in = input consumed by the command.
out = output written by the command, usually to a goal.
io = input and output, usually a goal that is read and then overwritten.

concepts.name: Parameter Types
concepts.definition: Type prefixes describe what sort of value a parameter expects.
details: Common AIRef types: Const, Goal, Sn, Op, Player, Text.
Op means the value type follows the operator family currently in use.

concepts.name: compareOp
concepts.definition: Comparison operator family used to compare constants, goals, or strategic numbers.
details: Bare operators default to constants, so > means the same thing as c:>.
Use g: prefixes for goal comparisons and s: prefixes for strategic-number comparisons.

concepts.name: mathOp
concepts.definition: Math operator family used to perform arithmetic and store the result in a goal or similar writable slot.
details: Unlike compareOp, the c:/g:/s: prefix is required.
Examples include c:+, g:+, and s:+.

concepts.name: typeOp
concepts.definition: Type operator used to force the next parameter to be interpreted as a constant, goal, or strategic number.
details: Valid prefixes are c:, g:, and s:.

concepts.name: Strategic Numbers
concepts.definition: Strategic numbers are mutable AI engine settings that influence built-in behavior and can sometimes be repurposed as spare storage.
details: AIRef documents 512 strategic-number slots from 0 to 511.
Only about 300 are actively used by the game according to the AIRef SN index summary.
AIRef recommends starting custom spare use from high IDs downward, noting that SN 511 has known DE issues.

concepts.name: Goals
concepts.definition: Goals are integer variables that the script can read and modify directly.
details: AIRef's data limits article lists goals as ranging from 1 to 16,000.
Many output parameters in advanced commands write to goals.

concepts.name: Defconsts
concepts.definition: Defconsts bind names to integer values or text strings so scripts can use readable identifiers instead of raw numbers.
details: AIRef explains that the underlying engine is fundamentally numeric, and defconsts help map readable tokens onto those numbers.
The data-limits article lists defconst numeric limits as -32768 to 32767, or a text string.

concepts.name: Direct Unit Control
concepts.definition: DUC is a UserPatch-origin AI scripting module for selecting specific units and controlling them more like a human player would.
details: AIRef's DUC guide frames it as manipulation of individual units and groups via IDs, searches, lists, and target commands.
It relies heavily on local-list and remote-list workflows.

concepts.name: Local List
concepts.definition: The DUC local list stores IDs of the AI player's own units and is used when inspecting or commanding those units.
details: AIRef's DUC guide says the local list can hold up to 240 IDs.
The data-limits article repeats the local-search length limit of 240.

concepts.name: Remote List
concepts.definition: The DUC remote list stores target IDs for any player's units, including enemies, allies, self targets, and Gaia.
details: AIRef's DUC guide says the remote list can hold up to 40 IDs.
Use the remote list when the object is the target of an order, even if it belongs to the AI player.

concepts.name: DUC Actions
concepts.definition: DUC actions are unit-control commands, usually up-* actions, that issue point, object, group, or search-derived orders to selected local-list units.
details: Typical examples include point targeting and object targeting commands such as up-target-point and up-target-objects.
They are often more powerful than default engine behavior but can be more expensive and stateful.

concepts.name: DUC Search / Reset
concepts.definition: Commands that clear DUC state or populate the local/remote search lists from map objects.
details: This family is the start of almost every reliable DUC flow.
Typical members include reset commands and find commands such as up-full-reset-search, up-find-local, up-find-remote, up-find-status-local, up-find-status-remote, and up-find-resource.

concepts.name: DUC Filters
concepts.definition: Commands that constrain subsequent DUC searches by distance, status, include/exclude criteria, or related search predicates.
details: Filters persist until reset, which is a common source of bugs.
Use this family when the symptom is 'the search found the wrong units' rather than 'the target command was wrong'.

concepts.name: DUC Selection / ID Scoping
concepts.definition: Commands that force the current local or remote scope to a specific object, ID, or current-object context.
details: This family is critical when the command should affect exactly one object rather than the whole current list.
Typical members include up-set-target-object, up-set-target-by-id, and up-add-object-by-id.

concepts.name: DUC State Capture / Measurement
concepts.definition: Commands that read search-state, points, object-data, distances, or pathing measurements into goals for later branching.
details: This family includes multi-goal writers and usually requires reserved consecutive goal blocks.
Typical members include up-get-search-state, up-get-point, up-get-object-data, up-get-point-distance, and up-get-path-distance.

concepts.name: DUC Point Targeting
concepts.definition: Commands that send currently selected local-list units to a point or issue point-based orders such as move, stop, unload, or gather-point updates.
details: Typical members include up-set-target-point, up-set-precise-target-point, and up-target-point.
This family often interacts with sn-target-point-adjustment and precise-coordinate workflows.

concepts.name: DUC Object Targeting
concepts.definition: Commands that issue an order from local-list units onto remote-list target objects.
details: Typical members include up-target-objects, often paired with remote-list population and narrowing.
Use this family for gather, attack, repair, garrison, or default-action behavior aimed at specific objects.

concepts.name: DUC List / Group Management
concepts.definition: Commands that sort, clean, trim, persist, or restore search-list contents rather than issuing the final order directly.
details: Typical members include up-clean-search, up-remove-objects, and group save/restore commands.
This family is where many one-unit narrowing and retry patterns live.

concepts.name: Classes / ClassId
concepts.definition: Classes group together similar types of units, such as infantry or warships.
details: AIRef positions classes as one of the main object-grouping abstractions alongside lines and sets.
Use the objects table to navigate from objects into class-oriented lookup.

concepts.name: Lines / LineId
concepts.definition: Lines group together a base unit and its upgraded versions so a script can count or target the line without hard-coding every upgrade state.
details: This is important for upgrade-stable counting like militia-line or scout-cavalry-line.

concepts.name: Sets / SetId
concepts.definition: Sets combine multiple related units or unit lines so they can be counted more easily as a broader family.
details: Sets are coarser than lines and help when related lines should be treated as one bucket.

concepts.name: Logical Operator Commands
concepts.definition: Logical operator commands combine or negate facts to control whether a rule's conditions evaluate true.
details: AIRef lists seven: and, nand, nor, not, or, xor, xnor.
They count toward the per-rule element limit.

concepts.name: Objects Table
concepts.definition: AIRef object table for unit, building, line, set, class, projectile, and dead-object lookups.
details: The page also explains dead-object IDs, projectile IDs, and the role of lines, sets, and classes.
Version-specific objects are marked and filtered on the page.

concepts.name: Technologies Table
concepts.definition: AIRef technology table for technology IDs and names.
details: Use it when researching or checking technology constants.

concepts.name: Data Limits
concepts.definition: Engine limits on rules, goals, strategic numbers, timers, flags, list sizes, and related scripting capacities.
details: Critical values from AIRef include: 10,000 rules, 32 elements per rule in DE, 1-16,000 goals, 1-50 timers, local DUC list length 240, remote DUC list length 40.

concepts.name: AI Command Performance Benchmarks
concepts.definition: AIRef benchmark article comparing relative command costs and lag thresholds for common search, sort, pathing, and DUC operations.
details: The article highlights that searches, sorts, pathing calls, and chat spam can become expensive quickly.
This is directly relevant when designing repeated DUC loops.

concepts.name: Intro to Commands
concepts.definition: AIRef primer explaining facts, actions, parameters, syntax prefixes, and operators.
details: This is the best first AIRef page for interpreting command signatures correctly.

concepts.name: AnyPlayer
concepts.definition: Parameter family for commands that accept a player selector rather than a raw object or numeric state value.
details: Use this family when a syntax slot refers to a player-like input such as any-enemy, self, ally, or target-player.
This is conceptually different from PlayerNumber, which is a numeric player identifier.

concepts.name: PlayerNumber
concepts.definition: Parameter family for numeric player identifiers produced or consumed by commands that work with concrete player numbers.
details: Do not confuse lobby color with AI player numbering.
DUC workflows and focus-player strategic numbers often need this family.

concepts.name: BuildingId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for building constants or building object identifiers used by build/count/check commands.
details: Resolve these through the AIRef objects table when the name is uncertain.
This family often appears in economy, military production, and defensive commands.

concepts.name: UnitId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for unit constants, object IDs, or class-based unit selectors depending on the command.
details: This family is broader than a single raw unit constant because some commands accept unit classes or line constants.
When the token is upgrade-stable, prefer a line or set if the command allows it.

concepts.name: TechId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for technology constants and technology identifiers used by research and technology-state commands.
details: Resolve unknown tech names through the AIRef technologies table.
Many tech constants use the ri- prefix in practice.

concepts.name: GoalId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for goal slots used as mutable integer storage or command outputs.
details: Many advanced commands write into goals, often consecutive blocks.
Goal parameters are one of the most common output families in DUC and point commands.

concepts.name: SnId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for strategic-number selectors and direct strategic-number references.
details: Use this when the syntax slot refers to which strategic number is being read or written, not to the value stored in it.

concepts.name: TimerId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for timer selectors used by enable, disable, and trigger-check commands.
details: AIRef's limits article documents timers 1 through 50.

concepts.name: SignalId
concepts.definition: Parameter family for scenario trigger signals and related scripted event hooks.
details: This family matters mainly in scenario-oriented AI work, not standard random-map openings.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.definition: Generic numeric parameter family used for counts, thresholds, distances, IDs, and operator-bound values.
details: The actual interpretation depends on the command and often on the operator prefix family.

concepts.name: String
concepts.definition: Text parameter family for quoted strings, mostly used in chat and text-related commands.
details: Strings are distinct from numeric defconst-style constants.

preconditions: The strategic number identifier must be defined and valid in this script context.
validated_patterns: Use it to suppress default AI subsystems before precise opening control.
Treat it as engine-behavior control first, not generic storage.
known_failure_modes: Wrong SN choice can silently fight your DUC logic by re-enabling built-in behavior.
anti_patterns: Using generic gatherer SNs alone to solve precise early-herdable control.

preconditions: Set sn-target-point-adjustment to adjust-precise (6) using SN id 292.
Provide absolute map coordinates scaled by 100.
validated_patterns: Set the precise target point, then issue up-target-point 0 action-move -1 -1.
Reset sn-target-point-adjustment back to adjust-middle (5) after the precise block.
known_failure_modes: Using SN id 294 instead of 292 leaves the command effectively imprecise.
Resetting adjustment to 0 instead of 5 can diverge from validated project behavior.
anti_patterns: Using tile coordinates instead of scaled precise coordinates.

preconditions: A valid stored object ID must already exist.
validated_patterns: Use it to set the current target object by stored ID.
TC transport garrison testing confirmed it as part of the working Barbarian-style garrison primitive.
known_failure_modes: It does not by itself constrain the local action scope for up-target-point.
anti_patterns: Relying on up-set-target-by-id alone to ensure only one livestock receives a point move.

preconditions: A valid stored object ID must already exist.
The destination list must be the correct local or remote scope for the next command.
validated_patterns: Reliable for adding the active herdable to search-remote before up-target-objects.
Useful as part of remote target setup.
known_failure_modes: Adding a single object to search-local after reset did not isolate local point-command scope in early owned-livestock probes.
anti_patterns: Assuming it replaces all local command scope when used alone with search-local.

preconditions: A current target object must already be set.
validated_patterns: Use it to store object-data-id and other current-object fields into goals.
known_failure_modes: Reading object data from the wrong current object because selection state was not refreshed.
anti_patterns: Calling it without a known current target object.

preconditions: Provide valid x/y point pairs and a reserved goal for the output.
validated_patterns: Store distances in goals, then branch on those stored goals with up-compare-goal for tie-sensitive logic.
known_failure_modes: Recomputing with up-point-distance later can disagree with the stored values in tie-sensitive cases.
anti_patterns: Logging up-get-point-distance and then branching by recomputing with up-point-distance.

preconditions: Compute the desired point first.
Assign builders and reset placement before building.
Use up-can-build-line as the placement guard when appropriate.
validated_patterns: For exact one-point house placement, pass the same x/y point pair as both line endpoints.
For multiple houses, save prior points, check separation with up-get-point-distance, and wait for pending count before advancing.
known_failure_modes: Two accepted build commands can still target overlapping or too-close foundations.
Later opening logic can steal builders if you do not wait for pending foundations.
anti_patterns: Treating an accepted build command as proof that a useful foundation exists.

preconditions: The referenced goal must already contain the value to branch on.
validated_patterns: Prefer it for branching on distances or derived values already stored in goals.
Use it with up-get-point-distance results for exact or tie-sensitive comparisons.
known_failure_modes: Branching on stale values because the producing command did not run in a prior rule pass.
anti_patterns: Recomputing with up-point-distance when the stored goal result is the thing you actually tested/logged.

preconditions: Be ready to rebuild local and remote scope afterward.
validated_patterns: Use it at the start of an independent DUC search phase.
Treat it as clearing actionable local scope as well as search contents.
known_failure_modes: Targeting immediately after reset without a fresh local scope leaks into undefined or unintended command behavior.
anti_patterns: Reset then up-target-point or up-target-objects without repopulating search-local.

preconditions: Reset or intentionally preserve filters depending on the search plan.
Use the right class/unit/line constant for the intended local scope.
validated_patterns: Rebuild search-local in the same rule before target commands.
Use small, purpose-specific searches rather than relying on stale local scope.
known_failure_modes: Persisted filters silently alter the result set.
Broad searches can capture more units than expected if not narrowed further.
anti_patterns: Assuming a prior rule's local list is still the correct command scope.

preconditions: Search one player's units at a time with the correct remote target model.
Reset or intentionally preserve filters depending on the search plan.
validated_patterns: Use it for visible Gaia herdables and other remote target acquisition.
Populate search-remote before object-target commands.
known_failure_modes: Remote visibility assumptions can fail when the object is undiscovered.
Mixing remote target state across players or object types without reset causes bad targeting.
anti_patterns: Treating remote search results as if they commandable local units.

notes: These entries confirm identifier presence and family, not full syntax or runtime semantics.
Use this inventory to avoid live AIRef dependency for token discovery and family classification.

lookup_workflows.problem: A command name is known, but its semantics or syntax are unclear.
steps: Check the commands index for category/type/version.
Read the command syntax with the intro-to-commands article in mind.
If the command is up-* or seems unit-control related, cross-check the DUC guide and command-experiments notes.

lookup_workflows.problem: A parameter token or syntax fragment is unfamiliar.
steps: Resolve whether the token is a direction prefix, type prefix, or operator family.
If it looks like an object grouping, pivot into classes, lines, or sets.

lookup_workflows.problem: A unit-control problem needs search-list, object-data, or targeting guidance.
steps: Start with the DUC concept and local/remote list entries.
Classify the problem into one of: search/reset, filters, selection scoping, state capture, point targeting, object targeting, or list/group management.
Read Enmipho's DUC guide section relevant to that family.
Cross-check local command probe notes before assuming runtime behavior.

lookup_workflows.problem: A script needs the right unit, building, line, set, class, or technology identifier.
steps: Use the objects or technologies table first.
If the problem is upgrade-stable counting, prefer lines or sets over raw object IDs.
If the problem is broad family selection, inspect classes.

preconditions: Reserve two consecutive goals for x and y output.
validated_patterns: Use it for position anchors such as position-self, position-center, and current target-object point reads.
known_failure_modes: Overwriting unrelated goals because the second consecutive goal was not reserved.
Confusing local and remote coordinate capture when the current target object was not set correctly first.
anti_patterns: Assuming a single goal write.
Reading remote-object point semantics without explicitly setting the remote target object first.

preconditions: Call it only after a search action.
Pass the first goal of a reserved four-goal consecutive block.
validated_patterns: Use it to inspect whether a search populated local or remote lists.
known_failure_modes: Passing the second/third/fourth goal of the block produces misleading state.
Treating the 'last search count' field as proof of post-filter current-list size.
anti_patterns: Using it as a post-filter count validator without a dedicated follow-up check.

preconditions: The x goal must be the first of a valid x/y point pair.
validated_patterns: Use it before point-distance or target-point-state logic.
Use it immediately before up-build place-point if testing place-point behavior.
known_failure_modes: Stale target-point state causing unrelated later commands to use the wrong point.
anti_patterns: Assuming it alone issues movement.
Assuming it fixes place-point reliability for all build cases; house placement preferred up-build-line in this project.

preconditions: The target search list must already be populated.
Choose an object-data field that matches the narrowing or sorting task.
validated_patterns: Sort by object-data-distance after setting a target point.
Use with object-data-index and follow-up removal when narrowing.
known_failure_modes: Sorting alone does not narrow the list to one object.
anti_patterns: Assuming index 0 is the only commanded object without explicit removal of the rest.

preconditions: The target search list must already be populated.
The comparison field must match the intended narrowing strategy.
validated_patterns: Use object-data-id comparisons to exclude or preserve a specific known object ID.
Use object-data-index after sorting only as part of a validated local narrowing sequence.
known_failure_modes: Index-based narrowing can be misleading if later commands still act on broader owned-livestock behavior.
Local last-search counts from up-get-search-state do not prove the post-filter current count.
anti_patterns: Treating object-data-index filtering as proof that only one object will receive a later point command.

preconditions: The referenced list and index must already exist.
validated_patterns: Use it before up-get-object-data or up-get-point on the current object.
known_failure_modes: Setting the target object does not necessarily shrink the underlying search list for later point-target commands.
anti_patterns: Assuming up-set-target-object search-local c:0 means only one local object is now in command scope.

preconditions: The local list must be explicitly populated in the same rule after the most recent reset.
For precise movement, sn-target-point-adjustment must be configured correctly.
validated_patterns: For precise movement, use SN id 292, set to adjust-precise (6), then issue the move and reset to adjust-middle (5).
For active livestock movement, rebuild search-local and filter by object-data-id before issuing the command.
After moving the active sheep, rebuild local livestock and issue action-stop to non-active spares.
known_failure_modes: Using stale local scope can command unintended units.
up-set-target-by-id alone does not isolate command scope.
Owned livestock can still exhibit group-follow behavior unless spares are explicitly stopped.
anti_patterns: Resetting then targeting without repopulating search-local.
Relying on index narrowing or current-target state alone for one-unit livestock movement.

preconditions: Local units to command must already be in search-local.
Target objects must already be in search-remote or otherwise set for remote targeting.
validated_patterns: For villager-to-active-herdable retask, put villagers in search-local and the active herdable ID in search-remote before issuing action-default.
For TC transport garrison, the validated pattern is local villager selection plus up-set-target-by-id on the TC followed by up-target-objects 1 action-garrison -1 -1.
known_failure_modes: Wrong local/remote ownership silently targets the wrong side of the command.
Ungarrison direction control remains unvalidated even when garrison itself works.
anti_patterns: Trying to issue object-targeting orders without explicitly rebuilding the correct remote scope.

preconditions: Set the intended target point first with up-set-target-point.
Use a valid escrow-state argument as the second parameter.
validated_patterns: Project uses the shape up-set-target-point build-point-x then up-build place-point goal-build-escrow-state c: house as the only valid candidate pattern worth testing.
known_failure_modes: Passing the coordinate goal as the second argument makes DE interpret it as an escrow state and fall back to generic placement.
Even with the better shape, exact starting-house placement proved unreliable versus up-build-line in isolated tests.
anti_patterns: up-build place-point point-x c: house
Using place-point for exact starting-house placement when up-build-line is available.

preconditions: Provide valid x/y point pairs.
validated_patterns: Use it for simple front/back or threshold-style branches when exact tie behavior is not critical.
known_failure_modes: It can disagree with stored up-get-point-distance values in tie-sensitive or exact-branch cases.
anti_patterns: Using it for exact or tie-sensitive selector logic after logging/storing distances with up-get-point-distance.

preconditions: The candidate build point must already be computed.
validated_patterns: Use it as a placement-stage guard before up-build-line.
known_failure_modes: A passing can-build check is not proof that multiple close build requests will yield separate useful foundations.
anti_patterns: Treating a positive can-build result as enough evidence to skip separation checks between consecutive buildings.

preconditions: A build request is about to be issued for the same building type.
validated_patterns: Set the intended builder count immediately before the build command.
Use explicit sequencing when multiple opening builds are involved.
known_failure_modes: Later build requests can absorb builders in unexpected ways if build steps overlap too much.
anti_patterns: Assuming builder assignment remains stable across overlapping opening build requests without serialization.

preconditions: A placement-oriented build sequence is about to begin.
validated_patterns: Call it in the exact-build sequence before up-build-line.
known_failure_modes: If omitted, placement state can be contaminated by earlier build attempts or implicit placement behavior.
anti_patterns: Treating it as optional in a precise multi-step placement probe.
